q: Plants use carbon dioxide and water in the presence of chlorophyll and light to compose glucose and oxygen.
e: This is the exact definition of photosynthesis provided in the textbook.

q: Photosynthesis takes place in the mitochondria of the green parts of plants but mainly in the leaves.
e: Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts of the green parts of plants, not the mitochondria.

q: The process of photosynthesis can be represented by the equation $6CO_2 + 12H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{Light energy, Chlorophyll}} C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 + 6H_2O$.
e: This is the exact balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis as shown in the textbook.

q: Most green parts of a plant can photosynthesize but the roots are best adapted for this function.
e: The leaves are best adapted for the function of photosynthesis, not the roots.

q: For photosynthesis efficiency, leaves need to have a large surface area to absorb light.
e: A large surface area is required to maximize light absorption for photosynthesis.

q: Leaves have veins including xylem and phloem to supply oxygen and a system for carrying away the photosynthetic products.
e: Veins including xylem and phloem supply water, not oxygen, to the leaf.

q: Most leaves are thin, flat structures supported by a petiole which supports the leaf blade to be angled to receive the maximum amount of sunlight.
e: This exact structural adaptation allows leaves to receive maximum sunlight.

q: The epidermis is a double layer of cells on the upper and lower surfaces of the leaf.
e: The epidermis is a single layer of cells on the upper and lower surfaces of the leaf.

q: In many plants, there is a thin waxy layer called the cuticle over the epidermis.
e: The cuticle is a thin waxy layer that covers the epidermis to reduce water loss.

q: In most dicotyledonous plants, the stomata occur only in the upper epidermis.
e: In most dicotyledonous plants, the stomata occur only in the lower epidermis.

q: In monocotyledonous plants, the stomata are equally distributed on both surfaces of the leaf.
e: This is the correct distribution of stomata in monocotyledonous plants.

q: The tissue between the upper and lower epidermis is called mesophyll.
e: Mesophyll is the tissue located between the upper and lower epidermis.

q: The palisade mesophyll cells are usually short and contain few chloroplasts.
e: The palisade mesophyll cells are usually long and contain many chloroplasts.

q: The spongy mesophyll cells vary in shape and are loosely arranged with many air spaces between them.
e: This loose arrangement with air spaces facilitates gas diffusion.

q: The major vein of the leaf is called the midrib, which is a continuation of the petiole.
e: The midrib is the major vein and is a direct continuation of the petiole.

q: In xylem, vessels are cylindrical, hollow and thin walled cells.
e: In xylem, vessels are cylindrical, hollow and thick walled cells.

q: The phloem consists of sieve tubes which are elongated cells and the transverse walls of sieve tubes are perforated sieve plates.
e: This accurately describes the structure of phloem tissue.

q: The upper epidermis helps to keep the leaf's shape and to reduce water loss.
e: This is one of the primary functions of the upper epidermis.

q: The epidermal cells are thick to prevent light from passing through.
e: The epidermal cells are thin to allow light to pass through to the mesophyll.

q: Chloroplasts are absent in the upper epidermal cells.
e: Upper epidermal cells lack chloroplasts to allow maximum light transmission.

q: Photosynthesis takes place mainly in the spongy mesophyll region.
e: Photosynthesis takes place mainly in the palisade mesophyll region.

q: The spongy mesophyll allows diffusion of carbon dioxide and oxygen in and out of mesophyll cells.
e: The air spaces in the spongy mesophyll facilitate this gas diffusion.

q: Xylem carries photosynthetic products to other parts of the plant.
e: Phloem transports photosynthetic products; xylem carries water and minerals.

q: The stoma is the site of gaseous exchange into and out of the leaf, located in the lower epidermis.
e: The stoma in the lower epidermis is the primary site for gaseous exchange.

q: Chloroplast is a membrane bound organelle containing chlorophyll a, b and other pigments.
e: This is the exact definition of a chloroplast's composition.

q: Plant cells contain chloroplasts which are red in colour.
e: Plant cells contain chloroplasts which are green in colour.

q: Chloroplasts found in higher plants are generally biconvex shaped.
e: Biconvex is the general shape of chloroplasts in higher plants.

q: The outer membrane of the chloroplast is a semi-porous membrane and is permeable to large molecules and ions.
e: The outer membrane is permeable to small molecules and ions, not large ones.

q: The intermembrane space is a thin space about 10-20 nm and it lies between the outer and the inner membranes of the chloroplast.
e: This accurately describes the location and size of the intermembrane space.

q: The inner membrane of the chloroplast forms a border to the stroma and regulates passage of materials in and out of the chloroplast.
e: This is the exact function of the inner membrane of the chloroplast.

q: The stroma is a protein rich aqueous fluid present within the outer membrane of the chloroplast.
e: The stroma is present within the inner membrane of the chloroplast.

q: The chloroplast DNA, ribosomes, the thylakoid system, starch granules and many proteins are found in the stroma.
e: These are the exact components listed as being found in the stroma.

q: The stroma is the site for the light reaction of photosynthesis.
e: The stroma is the site for the dark reaction of photosynthesis.

q: The thylakoids are suspended in the stroma and are membranous sacs which are arranged in stacks known as grana.
e: This accurately describes the structure and arrangement of thylakoids.

q: Each granum contains around 10-20 thylakoids.
e: This is the specific number of thylakoids per granum stated in the text.

q: The thylakoid membrane is the site for the dark reactions of photosynthesis.
e: The thylakoid membrane is the site for the light reactions of photosynthesis.

q: The green pigment chlorophyll is present on the membrane of thylakoid in the chloroplast.
e: Chlorophyll is located on the thylakoid membrane.

q: Chlorophyll reflects mostly the blue portion of light.
e: Chlorophyll reflects mostly the green portion of light.

q: The wavelengths of light blue-480 nm and red-700 nm are almost totally absorbed by chlorophyll.
e: These specific wavelengths are absorbed to transform light energy into chemical energy.

q: Photosynthesis is the process of conversion of light energy into chemical energy which can be utilized by the living organisms.
e: This is the exact definition of photosynthesis provided in the text.

q: Photosynthesis comprises of two phases: the light reaction and the dark reaction.
e: These are the two distinct phases of photosynthesis.

q: The light reaction takes place in the stroma of the chloroplast.
e: The light reaction takes place on the thylakoid membrane of the chloroplast.

q: The light reaction is a light-dependent process which includes light absorption, photolysis and release of oxygen and formation of ATP and NADPH.
e: This accurately lists the events of the light-dependent reaction.

q: The equation for the light reaction is $2H_2O + 2NADP^+ + 3ADP + 3P_i \rightarrow O_2 + 2NADPH + 3ATP$.
e: This is the exact chemical equation for the light reaction.

q: The dark reaction is also called the Krebs cycle.
e: The dark reaction is also called the Calvin cycle.

q: The dark reaction is a light-independent process in which sugar molecules are formed by using carbon dioxide with the help of ATP and NADPH.
e: This accurately describes the light-independent dark reaction.

q: The dark reaction converts six molecules of carbon dioxide into one sugar molecule i.e. glucose.
e: This is the exact outcome of the dark reaction described in the text.

q: The equation for the dark reaction is $6CO_2 + 18ATP + 12NADPH \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6H_2O + 18ADP + 18P_i + 12NADP^+$.
e: This is the exact chemical equation for the dark reaction.

q: In the light reaction, the water molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen.
e: This process is known as photolysis and occurs during the light reaction.

q: In the dark reaction, photolysis occurs.
e: Photolysis occurs in the light reaction, not the dark reaction.

q: The rate of photosynthesis varies according to controlling factors such as light intensity, temperature and carbon dioxide concentration.
e: These are the three main controlling factors listed for photosynthesis.

q: As the light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases until it reaches a maximum rate.
e: This accurately describes the effect of light intensity on photosynthesis.

q: Under bright light, the rate of photosynthesis increases with a rise in temperature up to a maximum temperature of around 50°C.
e: The maximum temperature for photosynthesis is around 40°C, not 50°C.

q: Beyond the maximum temperature, the rate of photosynthesis drops rapidly.
e: Enzymes denature beyond the optimum temperature, causing a rapid drop in rate.

q: The concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is about 0.4%.
e: The concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is about 0.04%.

q: Under experimental conditions, the rate of photosynthesis increases with higher carbon dioxide concentration up to a certain level.
e: Increasing CO2 concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis up to a saturation point.

q: There are four requirements of photosynthesis, namely chlorophyll, light, carbon dioxide and water.
e: These are the exact four requirements listed in the textbook.

q: In investigations for requirements of photosynthesis, the plants must first be destarched.
e: Destarching ensures that any starch detected is newly formed during the experiment.

q: Variegated leaves which have chlorophyll as green patches can be found in plants like Coleus, spiderwort and croton.
e: These are the exact examples of plants with variegated leaves provided.

q: The leaves are destarched by placing the plant in the dark for 2-3 days.
e: This is the exact method and duration for destarching described in the text.

q: In the investigation for chlorophyll, only the green patches previously will turn blue-black with iodine solution.
e: The green patches contain chlorophyll and thus produce starch, turning blue-black.

q: In the investigation for light, a portion of green leaf is sandwiched between two pieces of black paper or black tape or aluminium foil.
e: This is the exact procedure to block light from a portion of the leaf.

q: In the investigation for light, the parts with black paper will turn blue-black.
e: The parts with black paper will remain brown because no starch was produced.

q: In the investigation for carbon dioxide, $NaHCO_3$ (sodium hydrogen carbonate) is put inside set-up A for producing carbon dioxide.
e: Sodium hydrogen carbonate is used to provide a source of carbon dioxide.

q: In the investigation for carbon dioxide, $NaOH$ (sodium hydroxide) is put inside set-up B to produce carbon dioxide.
e: NaOH (sodium hydroxide) is used to absorb carbon dioxide, not produce it.

q: The leaf from the plant in which $NaHCO_3$ has been placed will turn blue-black.
e: This leaf received carbon dioxide, allowing photosynthesis and starch production.
